extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; practicing journalists interested in press ethics and style
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpt from a history of journalism outlining professional motives, ethics, style guidance, and the institutional role of newspapers; mixes normative claims (what good journalism is) with historical examples and a prescriptive word-list. Useful for evaluating historical and contemporary journalistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality of reporters / diversity of accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Considered as individuals, no two are alike; a regiment of reporters will hear the same speech or witness the same convention, yet what they write will have such rare diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that reporters should bring their individual intellects and perspectives to coverage; accept and value differing accounts of the same event rather than strict uniformity. This suggests a criterion for judging reportage: the presence of distinct, thoughtful perspective rather than identical, formulaic copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of the 'game' (intrinsic motivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many newspaper men explain their attraction to the calling by the 'love of the game.' The flavor of adventure is never lacking in successful journalism because underlying it is the consciousness that the public is being served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic vocation is framed as driven by passion for the work and the adventure of reporting. As an evaluative criterion, enthusiasm and sustained commitment to reporting are markers of professionalism; the passage treats this intrinsic motivation as foundational to effective journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missionary spirit / public responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: There is always a strong belief that this country is different ... the missionary spirit — the sense of personal responsibility for the right conduct of our government and our people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should hold a sense of public mission: to serve the public weal and hold government and citizens accountable. The book treats this 'missionary spirit' as an implicit ethical standard guiding reporting and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to paper and unwritten professional code
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (e.g., Gregory T. Humes) show reporters who 'thought first of his paper' and whose conduct 'dignified' the occupation by 'complete fidelity to its highest standards and its unwritten code.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional loyalty and fidelity—placing duty to inform the public and the news organization before personal concerns—are held up as virtues. The text uses concrete examples (injured correspondents dictating copy, mortally injured reporter requesting his paper be notified) as standards of conduct to emulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of immediacy / justification for immediate reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argued immediate reporting of a railway wreck wasn't necessary, but the author counters that the American public expects prompt information; immediate reporting serves the public in crowded urban or remote rural contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediacy is defended as a journalistic requirement: even when facts will later be revealed by formal inquiry, timely reporting meets public needs and sustains public trust. Use of urgency as a criterion must still be balanced with accuracy, but the passage foregrounds timeliness as a professional norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial steadiness and avoidance of sensational incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: William Bradford and his successors 'conducted their journals with an ability which perfectly sustained them; and with no one did they go to extreme lengths ... unmarked by those incidents which arrest the attention by agitating the passions of mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and proprietors are praised for steady, reputable management and resisting sensationalism. As a standard, newspapers should aim for sustainable credibility and honorable conduct rather than exploiting passion-stirring incidents for attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the press as essential to public deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial of Zenger 'marked a complete change' and was 'an achievement for the freedom of the press,' enabling the creation of an implement for the people; had Zenger been convicted, the development of free discussion would have been delayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press freedom—especially the right to print the truth about public questions—is presented as a foundational normative standard for judging the press's role in society; safeguard of freedom is a criterion for a healthy press environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bryant's Index Expurgatorius (words and usages to avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: A compiled list of words and phrases Bryant considered unsuitable for newspaper use (examples: 'darky' for 'negro'; 'poetess'; avoid passives like 'is being done'; prefer 'dinner' to 'banquet'; avoid unnecessary euphemisms or inflated diction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a prescriptive style guide: editors and reporters should avoid archaic, euphemistic, racist, or pretentious vocabulary and prefer clear, plain, and non-offensive terms; the book reproduces Bryant's list as concrete editorial rules and substitution suggestions. The list is extensive and intended as practical copy-edit guidance compiled by an experienced editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match form to public appetite and evolve presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Early news pamphlets were crude and disjointed; 'the appetite for news is whetted and increased efforts are made to appease it' — pamphlets later 'begin to assume a more definite form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News producers should refine format and presentation to meet growing public demand; evolution from crude fragments to structured forms is presented as a natural improvement path. As a criterion, assess whether the publication's form suits audience needs and shows editorial development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional industry and honorable liberality in editorial conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Bradford 'pursued a long career of creditable industry, unmarked by those incidents which arrest the attention ...' and 'managed the concerns of their offices generally with steady success and honorable liberality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term professional competence, fair business conduct, and liberal (fair-minded) editorial practices are standards by which publishers/editors are praised; look for sustained stewardship and integrity in judging editorial leadership.
